activities.anchor: Civilisation is a chain reaction. Farming produces
activities.caption: pair each link with its role in the reaction
activities.name: ccChainMatch

config.prompt: The chain reaction, link by link — pair each with its role:

pairs.right: what farming produces, letting some people stop farming
scribes, smiths, priests and soldiers, freed from the fields
what specialists build when surplus concentrates
what cities need once they exist

config.why: Every cradle of civilisation, from the Nile to the Indus, runs the same sequence with local accents — farming, surplus, specialists, cities, states.

activities.anchor: The puzzle is why the reaction took so long
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the long wait
activities.name: ccDeepEstimate

config.prompt: Anatomically modern humans have existed for roughly how many years?
config.why: Roughly 300,000 years — yet farming begins only about 12,000 years ago and the first cities about 6,000: humans spent 95% of their species' history not building civilisations, until the end of the last Ice Age made wild cereals dense enough to tend.
config.context: Farming was invented independently at least half a dozen times — conditions, not a single genius, start the reaction.

activities.anchor: The archaeologist V. Gordon Childe called it a
activities.caption: find the faulty line — the Neolithic balance sheet
activities.name: ccNeolithicSpot

config.prompt: One line of this Neolithic balance sheet is wrong — click it:
lines: Domesticating wheat, barley, rice and maize meant people could stay put, store food and support more children.
Settled mothers wean earlier than carrying-foragers, which raised birth spacing.
Stored grain became wealth that could be owned, stolen and defended.
Skeletons show early farmers were typically taller and better-fed than their hunter ancestors.
Dense settled populations became disease incubators, with infections jumping from domesticated animals.
config.correction: Skeletons show early farmers were typically shorter and worse-fed than their hunter ancestors — farming was less a leap upward than a trap that paid in numbers.
config.why: The transition took centuries, but Childe's label sticks for its consequences: villages swelled into towns, hierarchies grew around the granary, and the costs were real — farmers paid in bodies and won in numbers.

activities.anchor: went first because irrigation there turned silt into wheat
activities.caption: file each achievement under its cradle
activities.name: ccCradlesBuckets

config.prompt: Six cradles, one pattern — file each exhibit:

items.label: Uruk held tens of thousands by about 3400–3100 BCE — the first true city
stepped ziggurats and rival city-states that traded as ferociously as they fought
a flood that arrived almost punctually, so a single state could organise it
the Giza pyramids, tallest structures on Earth for the next four millennia
Harappa and Mohenjo-daro on precise street grids with covered drains
standardised brick sizes and weights — and oddly, no evidence of kings or palaces

config.why: Six regions, three continents, no contact between them — one pattern. Which is why historians have retired 'the cradle': civilisation is something humans do when rivers and grain cooperate, not a torch handed down from a single origin.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — where writing comes from
activities.name: ccCuneiformCloze

config.text: Cuneiform — wedges pressed in clay — began in Uruk around %%0%% as %%1%%: receipts for grain, beer and livestock. Only centuries of reuse turned the system literary, eventually producing the %%2%%, the world's oldest great work of literature.
config.hint: The earliest tablets are tallies and receipts, not poems — the counting came first.

activities.anchor: The Bronze Age world — palace economies wired together by trade
activities.caption: true or false — the collapse, read closely
activities.name: ccBronzeJudge

statements.s: The Bronze Age palace economies were wired together by long-distance trade in copper and tin.
statements.why: Interdependence is efficient until any link breaks.

statements.s: Ugarit burned with its tablets still in the oven; the Hittite empire vanished.
statements.why: The cascade ran around 1200–1150 BCE — drought, migrations and raids together.

statements.s: Egypt fell with the rest, disappearing from the record around 1177 BCE.
statements.why: Egypt alone survived — recording its victories against the mysterious 'Sea Peoples' at Medinet Habu in 1177 BCE.

statements.s: A world built over two millennia came apart in about a generation.
statements.why: The classic lesson: complex systems fail fast.

activities.caption: line up the empires, earliest first
activities.name: ccEmpiresOrder

config.prompt: From collapse to empire — order these, earliest first:
items: Assyria ruled by terror and deportations
Persia's template — Cyrus, the Royal Road, satraps audited from the centre — from ~550 BCE
Rome extends citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants — 212 CE
the western half 'falls' as Odoacer deposes one more emperor — 476 CE
config.why: The recovery showed the opposite virtue of the collapse: Persia and then Rome scaled government itself — roads, governors and law — across three continents, and Rome's eastern half outlived its western by a thousand years.

activities.anchor: Egypt ran the same machine on a more reliable river
activities.caption: drag the divider — two rivers, two politics
activities.name: ccNileCompare

config.prompt: Same machine, different rivers — drag the divider:

before.label: Mesopotamia — the Tigris and Euphrates
before.text: Irrigation turned silt into wheat on an industrial scale, but the canals needed corvée labour and the water was local — so rival city-states traded and fought, rations of bread and beer were paid from temple granaries, and grain collected as tax kept the whole ledger balanced.

after.label: Egypt — the Nile
after.text: A flood gentle, predictable and on planting season meant one state, not rivals, could plan around it; surveying fields after each flood made Egypt the birthplace of practical geometry, and the pyramids were logistics projects — feeding 10,000 or more workers on an industrial schedule — as much as monuments.

config.why: Infrastructure writes the politics: where water needed cooperation at scale, strong central states formed; where irrigation was local, competitive city-states did.
